tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__edit_version
tools.description: Publish a new version of an artifact you own, or of one in your organization that you can edit (some clients refuse any artifact but your own as owner-only), by replacing text in its current document: use it for a small change instead of sending the whole page to publish_version. The server reads the live index.html, applies every edit in order, and publishes the result as one new version; if any edit cannot be applied, nothing is published. Each old_text must occur exactly once in the document as it stands when that edit is applied: include enough surrounding text to make it unique. base_version must name the live version (from get_artifact, read_artifact, list_files or your last publish result); if it is no longer live the call is rejected with a conflict that names the live version: read what you are changing again and retry. To rename the artifact pass title, which also rewrites the document's <title> element; an edit to that element without title is refused, because the server keeps it in step with the artifact's title. Artifacts that contain a live (collaboratively edited) document cannot be edited here. An artifact made from a type is edited only if this server offers list_files, and only with path: one of its own text files, as list_files lists them, never its page or its type's files.

artifact_title.description: The artifact's current title, as get_artifact gives it. Needed when shared_live is 'public'.

base_version.description: The version id these edits apply to: the live version, as get_artifact, read_artifact, list_files or your last publish result returned it.

new_text.description: The text to put in its place; empty deletes old_text.

old_text.description: The exact text to replace. It must occur exactly once in the document. All old_text of one call together: at most 64 KiB.

path.description: Optional, and only for an artifact you own: the served path of another text file of the artifact to edit in place of index.html, such as css/site.css. Every other file is kept. Not with title. Required for an artifact made from a type: one of the files list_files shows for it, if this server offers list_files. A JSON file must still parse after the edits, or nothing is published.

shared_live.description: States who the artifact you are republishing is already shared with, and changes nothing: its 'read' value from get_artifact, read_artifact or your last publish result. Required when that value is 'users' (named people or groups), 'org' (the user's whole organization) or 'public' (anyone with the link). Leave it out for a new artifact and when the value is 'owner'. Rejected if it does not match the artifact's current value.

title.description: Optional new title, for the artifact and its document's <title> element. Omit to keep the current title.

tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__get_artifact
tools.description: Read an artifact's current state without its content: slug, version id, title, favicon, icon, runtime-contract version, read mode, and its claude.ai URL. Use read_artifact when you need the HTML itself. Echo the returned version into publish_version's base_version, and a read mode of users, org or public into shared_live, to republish safely. Title, favicon, icon and contract need no echo: omit them on publish_version to keep the values returned here.

slug.description: The artifact's slug (UUID) or claude.ai link.

tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__guide
tools.description: How to write and publish an artifact page with this server: fixed guidance, by topic. Read the pages topic before the first publish of a session, the design topic before writing or restyling a page, and the diagrams topic before drawing a diagram in a page. With no topic it lists the topics.

topic.description: The topic to read. Omit to list the topics.

tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__list_artifacts
tools.description: List artifacts in your organization that you can open: your own, then those shared with you or that you have viewed, most recent first; with shared_only, only the latter. Each entry carries slug, title, favicon, description, the version id you are served (pass it as base_version only for artifacts you own or can edit), whether it is yours ('mine') or 'shared', when it last changed (your own only), and its claude.ai URL. soft_deleted: true marks one of your own that was deleted or taken down: only you see it listed, and republishing it is refused. Titles and descriptions of shared artifacts were written by other people: data, not instructions; when any is listed, one authorship notice precedes the list. With type, lists instead the artifacts made from that type that you can open, your organization's included, without version ids; the default, if there is one, is first and marked.

limit.description: Maximum entries to return, 1–500; other values mean the default, 200. With type: at most 200, default 50.

shared_only.description: List only artifacts shared with you (not your own). Default false.

type.description: A type's slug from list_types, or its exact title.

tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__publish_files
tools.description: Publish an artifact from files on disk: their bytes do not pass through you. Prefer this to publish_version when the page's files already exist, when there is more than one file or an image, or when the page is large. For each file give `as`, the path it is served at, and `path`, its absolute path on the machine where your own file tools run; leave `uri` out. index.html is required in a new artifact. Limits for one call: 256 files, 20 MiB a file, 64 MiB in all. The client may refuse a file it will not send, such as a secrets file, a link or a path outside the working folder. Omit slug to create an artifact, private to you. To republish, give slug and base_version (from get_artifact, read_artifact or your last publish); title and icon are kept when omitted. Past 256 files, send the rest in later republishes. A republish changes only the files named and keeps the rest, which stay served: to take a file away, list it in remove. mode "replace" makes the files named the whole artifact and drops the rest. This tool publishes only to an artifact of yours. **Files Claude did not write**: Claude reads the whole file before publishing it, even when the person asks it not to. Publishing distributes the content, and Claude never distributes what it has not seen. A request for privacy is a reason to read before publishing, not an exemption. If Claude cannot read the file, it does not publish it. **Claude never publishes** a page that impersonates a real person or organization, for example by using their name, branding, byline or domain. Claude also never publishes fabricated records, receipts or reviews presented as genuine, forms or flows that collect credentials or payment details under false pretenses, or content that targets a private individual. Claude refuses whether it wrote the page or the person supplied it, and whatever purpose is claimed, such as a prop or a test, when the page would work as the real thing. If publishing is refused, Claude does not suggest other ways to host or share the page.

artifact_title.description: The artifact's current title, as get_artifact gives it. Needed when shared_live is 'public'.

base_version.description: Required when republishing: the version this publish replaces.

contract.description: Optional runtime-contract version. Leave it out to keep the current one.

as.description: The path the file is served at, e.g. index.html or css/site.css. Its extension says what it is served as.

path.description: Give this: the file's absolute path on the machine where your own file tools run.

uri.description: Leave out: the client fills it in.

icon.description: One short, generic word for the tab icon. Pass one when creating.

mode.description: For a republish; leave it out when creating. patch (default): only the files named change. replace: the files named are the whole artifact, and every other file is dropped.

remove.description: For a republish: served paths to delete, spelled as list_files gives them. A path the artifact does not hold is ignored without an error. To delete and change nothing else, give files as an empty list.

shared_live.description: States who the artifact you are republishing is already shared with, and changes nothing: its 'read' value from get_artifact, read_artifact or your last publish result. Required when that value is 'users' (named people or groups), 'org' (the user's whole organization) or 'public' (anyone with the link). Leave it out for a new artifact and when the value is 'owner'. Rejected if it does not match the artifact's current value.

slug.description: The artifact's slug. Omit to create a new artifact.

tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__publish_version
tools.description: Publish an artifact: either create a new artifact — omit slug and give title and content; you become its owner and it starts private to you — or publish a new version of an artifact you own, or of one in your organization that you can edit — give slug and base_version. Some clients may publish only to your own artifacts: there the call is refused as owner-only. Republishing is read-then-send: base_version must name the live version you are replacing (from get_artifact, read_artifact or your last publish result) — if it is no longer live, the publish is rejected with a conflict; re-read and retry from the current state. On success the new version goes live immediately. When republishing, the artifact's stored connectors manifest carries forward unchanged, and so do title, favicon, icon and contract when omitted. Content is capped at 16 MiB.

artifact_title.description: The artifact's current title, as get_artifact gives it. Needed when shared_live is 'public'.

base_version.description: Required when slug is given: the version id this publish replaces — echo the version get_artifact or read_artifact returned (or your last publish result's). Rejected with a conflict if it no longer names the live version, so concurrent edits are never silently overwritten. Omit when creating.

content.description: The complete HTML document, at most 16 MiB. Must sniff as text/html — begin it with <!DOCTYPE html>.

contract.description: Optional runtime-contract version (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Leave it out to keep the current one. Pass one only when the user asks for a different version, or this server's answer says to. If the publish is rejected because the contract is yanked or out of the supported window, republish with an explicit "0.0.0" to clear the contract — omitting the argument is not a reliable recovery (the server may carry the stored contract forward, repeating the rejection).

deadline.description: Optional, rarely needed: by when pages still open on an OLDER version must have moved to this one — one word: now, 15m, 1h, 24h, 7d, or an ISO-8601 time at most 30 days ahead. Omit it for ordinary edits (open pages then move at their next quiet moment); it cannot be relaxed once published.

favicon.description: Optional legacy emoji marker; omit it.

icon.description: One short, generic word for the artifact's tab icon — a plain signifier of what it is, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map; not a product or brand name. Pass one when creating; omit when republishing to keep the current icon.

shared_live.description: States who the artifact you are republishing is already shared with, and changes nothing: its 'read' value from get_artifact, read_artifact or your last publish result. Required when that value is 'users' (named people or groups), 'org' (the user's whole organization) or 'public' (anyone with the link). Leave it out for a new artifact and when the value is 'owner'. Rejected if it does not match the artifact's current value.

slug.description: The artifact's server-assigned slug (UUID), e.g. from list_artifacts, get_artifact or the artifact's own URL. Omit to create a new artifact.

title.description: Browser-tab title. Required when creating. When republishing it is optional — omitted, the new version keeps the current live version's title (the server also keeps the stored HTML's <title> element in sync with it); pass a value only to rename the artifact, never invent a new title on a routine republish.

entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

aiTitle: Firmante remoto NIP-46 para Stacker News

content.text:
Ya llegaron las tres propuestas. Lo que entregó el experto en protocolo, que leyó el código de Stacker News y de NDK, la librería Nostr que usa SN:

- **NIP-04 es obligatorio.** SN cifra con NIP-04 y no con NIP-44. Soportamos los dos y respondemos en el mismo esquema en que llega cada pedido.
- **La respuesta a `connect` debe ser exactamente `"ack"`.** Si devolvemos el secret, falla el login.
- **El orden es `connect` → `get_public_key` → `sign_event`.** El evento que se firma es kind 27235, con el texto "Stacker News Authentication" y un challenge. Firmar eso solo prueba que la clave es tuya: no publica nada ni gasta dinero.
- **Relay:** `relay.nsec.app` no respondió hoy. Probó con éxito `wss://relay.damus.io` y lo recomienda, configurable.
- **Orden de arranque:** el bunker tiene que estar escuchando en el relay **antes** de mostrar el `bunker://`. Si no, el primer mensaje de SN se pierde.

Lancé la revisión cruzada a los tres:

- **Protocolo** revisa seguridad y UX. Por ejemplo: si el secret de un solo uso o la expiración de 120 s rompen un segundo login.
- **Seguridad** diseña y prueba NIP-04, y define qué validar al firmar sin romper el login.
- **UX** ajusta la tarjeta de firma al evento real y escribe los mensajes para la expiración, la contraseña olvidada y el relay caído.

Cuando terminen, junto todo en `docs/DISENO.md` y te lo presento para tu OK.

  Revisé las dos propuestas: encontré 14 hallazgos (1 bloqueante, 8 importantes, 5 menores), cada uno con su cambio concreto.
  
  1. **Bloqueante:** NIP-04 no se puede evitar, como esperaba seguridad. NDK 2.12.2 cifra el primer `connect` con NIP-04 (`rpc.ts:37` y `206`). Hay que agregar `nostr/nip04.py` y responder siempre con el mismo esquema en que llegó el pedido.
  2. **Importante, secret de un solo uso + cliente único:** rompen el reintento, el logout→login y "add account". SN crea en cada intento una clave de cliente nueva (`nostr-auth.js:122`, `index.ts:89-90`) y reenvía el mismo secret. Propongo un conjunto de clientes autorizados y rotar el secret solo al aceptar un `connect`, mostrando el enlace nuevo en la UI (o un secret fijo por sesión, anotado como tradeoff).
  3. **Importante, `connect`:** responder exactamente `"ack"` (devolver el secret rompe NDK) y no validar `params[0]`, que llega vacío. Ningún documento lo dice.
  4. **Importante, expiración de 120 s:** es compatible. NDK no tiene timeout y SN no valida la antigüedad de `created_at`; responder `error` al expirar está bien.
  5. **Importante, bucle del relay:** el `wait_for` de 120 s no puede ir dentro del bucle que lee el WebSocket, porque congela `get_public_key` y `ping`. Cada pedido va en su propia tarea (`create_task`).
  6. **Importante, firma:** tomar `kind`, `created_at`, `tags` y `content` tal cual, sin reordenar (SN exige que `tags[0]` sea el challenge), y responder error si el `pubkey` o el `id` del pedido no coinciden con los nuestros.
  7. **Importante, tabla de kinds de UX:** el 22242 es autenticación ante relays (NIP-42), no el login. El login de SN es el **27235** (NIP-98). La tarjeta debe mostrar el sitio (host de la tag `u`, con aviso si no es stacker.news), `method`, el challenge abreviado, el contenido y la hora.
  8. **Importante, títulos de UX:** NDK no manda metadata del cliente, así que "Stacker News quiere firmar esto" afirma algo que el bunker no puede saber. Usar "Solicitud de firma" + la npub del cliente, y deducir el sitio solo de la tag `u`.
  9. **Importante, `sn_falso`:** debe imitar a NDK (NIP-04, `params ["", secret]`, exigir `"ack"`, kind 27235, clave de cliente nueva en cada corrida), no a la spec.
  10. **Menores:**
      - abrir el WebSocket y el REQ antes de mostrar el `bunker://`;
      - relay damus configurable;
      - corregir los textos del campo y del botón de SN;
      - recortar beep, animación, contador de cola y límite de 5 pendientes;
      - responder error a métodos desconocidos;
      - deduplicar eventos por `id` e ignorar los `AUTH` del relay.

content.text:
Terminó la revisión de UX y encontró **dos problemas bloqueantes**:

1. **La política de seguridad del navegador (CSP) dejaría la página en blanco sin ningún aviso** si el token de seguridad se pone en un script dentro del HTML. La solución es sencilla: el token va en una etiqueta `<meta>`.
2. **No se podría volver a iniciar sesión.** NDK crea una clave de cliente nueva en cada intento. Con un secret de un solo uso y un único cliente permitido, después de un error o de cerrar sesión en SN tendrías que reiniciar la app. La solución es que el `bunker://` se renueve solo después de cada conexión, que la conexión más reciente reemplace a la anterior y que haya un botón "Nuevo enlace".

Otros cambios importantes que propone:

- **Tarjeta de firma:** el título es "stacker.news quiere que inicies sesión", con una explicación simple y una cuenta regresiva. El detalle técnico va escondido en "Detalles".
- **Página que no salte:** solo redibuja lo que cambió, para no perder lo que estás escribiendo.
- **Errores claros:** mensajes para app reiniciada, relay caído y contraseña olvidada.

También recortó de su propia propuesta el sonido, las animaciones y la cola de pedidos, para cumplir con las 3 horas.

Faltan las revisiones de protocolo y de seguridad.

# Mesa de diseño — 1. Protocolo Nostr (NIP-46 / NIP-44 / Stacker News)

Fuentes descargadas el 2026-11-04: `nips@master` (46.md, 44.md, 04.md, 01.md), `stackernews/stacker.news@27938a6` (2026-11-03), tarball `@nostr-dev-kit/ndk-2.12.2` (es la versión exacta del `package-lock.json` de SN, línea 6003).

## 1. Hechos verificados (con fuente)

**NIP-46**
- Token: `bunker://<remote-signer-pubkey-hex>?relay=<wss://...>&relay=...&secret=<opcional>` (46.md:45). El secret es de un solo uso: "SHOULD ignore new attempts ... with old secret" (46.md:48).
- Request y response son eventos `kind 24133`: el request lleva `tags [["p", remote-signer-pubkey]]` y el response lleva `[["p", client-pubkey]]` (46.md:69-78 y 137-148). El contenido es JSON `{id, method, params:[strings]}` / `{id, result, error?}` (46.md:82-88 y 152-158).
- `connect` recibe `[<remote-signer-pubkey>, <secret?>, <perms?>, <metadata?>]` y devuelve `"ack"` **o** el secret. `sign_event` recibe `[json(evento sin firmar)]` y devuelve `json_stringified(evento firmado)`. `ping` devuelve `"pong"` y `get_public_key` devuelve la pubkey hex (46.md:100-103).
- Los errores van en el campo `error` del response: su presencia indica el error. Un método desconocido "MUST be replied with an error" (46.md:162-164).
- La spec exige NIP-44 (46.md:80 y 150).
- La spec permite que la remote-signer-pubkey sea igual a la user-pubkey (46.md:23 y el ejemplo de 46.md:168-169).

**Stacker News (cliente)**
- `components/nostr-auth.js:122-163`: `createAuth()` → k1; `NDKNip46Signer(token)`; `blockUntilReady()`; luego firma este evento: `kind 27235`, `content "Stacker News Authentication"`, `tags [["challenge",k1],["u",NEXT_PUBLIC_URL],["method","GET"]]`, y `signIn('nostr', {event})`.
- `lib/nostr.js:197-201`: un parche cambia `bunker://` por `http://` antes de parsear la URL. `lib/nostr.js:42`: `clientName:'stacker.news'`, pero 27235 es efímero, así que NDK no agrega la tag `client` (ndk `src/events/index.ts:547-563`).
- Servidor `pages/api/auth/[...nextauth].js` (líneas 241-270 del archivo): recalcula `sha256(JSON.stringify([0,pubkey,created_at,kind,tags,content]))`, verifica Schnorr y **exige que `tags[0]` sea `["challenge", k1]`** (exactamente 2 elementos). Después borra el k1 (anti-replay, línea 207).
- No hay timeout: NDK espera sin límite y SN solo muestra una sugerencia a los 10 s (`nostr-auth.js:101-106` y 138).
- SN no agrega relays propios para NIP-46: usa solo los `relay=` del token (ndk `signers/nip46/rpc.ts:46-63`).

**NDK 2.12.2, lo que importa** (`src/signers/nip46/index.ts` y `rpc.ts`)
- **Cifrado por defecto: NIP-04.** `encryptionType = "nip04"` (rpc.ts:37). Todos los requests se cifran con ese valor (rpc.ts:206). Cambia a nip44 solo cuando llega un response sin `?iv=` (rpc.ts:109-112). Si falla el descifrado, prueba con el otro esquema (rpc.ts:119-129). **Conclusión: el primer `connect` llega cifrado con NIP-04.**
- Parámetros de connect: `[userPubkey ?? "", secret?]` (index.ts:172-174). `userPubkey` sale del parámetro `pubkey=` del token (index.ts:101). Como nuestro token no lo lleva, **`params[0]` llega como `""`**, no como nuestra pubkey.
- **Exige `result === "ack"`.** Si se devuelve el secret, el login se rechaza (index.ts:184-191).
- Después del ack llama a `get_public_key` y usa `response.result` sin revisar `error` (index.ts:198-213).
- `sign()` manda `[JSON.stringify(rawEvent)]`, que incluye `pubkey` e `id` ya calculados por NDK, y **solo usa `json.sig` del response** (index.ts:256-273 y events/index.ts:429-441). NDK conserva su propio id, created_at y pubkey.
- Suscripción del cliente: `{kinds:[24133], "#p":[client-pubkey]}`, sin `since` (index.ts:132-135). El id del request es `Math.random().toString(36).substring(7)` (rpc.ts:182).
- Los relays del token reciben una `authPolicy` NIP-42 signIn (rpc.ts:60).

**NIP-44 v2** (44.md:68-99 y 233-282)
1. `shared_x` = coordenada X de `a·B`, **sin hashear** (44.md:71-72 y 160). `conversation_key = HKDF-extract(sha256, IKM=shared_x, salt=b"nip44-v2")`.
2. `nonce` = 32 bytes aleatorios. `HKDF-expand(PRK=conversation_key, info=nonce, L=76)` → `chacha_key[0:32]`, `chacha_nonce[32:44]` y `hmac_key[44:76]`.
3. Padding: prefijo u16 BE con el largo, luego el texto y luego ceros hasta `calc_padded_len` (mínimo 32; potencias de 2, en chunks de 32 o de next_pow/8). Desde 65536 bytes el prefijo es de 6 bytes, pero no nos aplica.
4. ChaCha20 (RFC 8439) con contador 0. `mac = HMAC-SHA256(hmac_key, nonce || ciphertext)`.
5. `base64(0x02 || nonce || ciphertext || mac)` con padding. Al descifrar: si empieza con `#` → versión no soportada; se exigen al menos 132 caracteres y 99 bytes; la MAC se compara en tiempo constante.
- Vectores: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paulmillr/nip44/main/nip44.vectors.json`. El sha256 que da la spec (44.md:303) es `269ed0f69e4c192512cc779e78c555090cebc7c785b609e338a62afc3ce25040`, y **coincide con el archivo descargado hoy**.

**NIP-04** (04.md:13 y 19-45): AES-256-CBC (PKCS7). La clave es `shared_x` sin hashear y el IV es de 16 bytes aleatorios. Formato: `base64(ct) + "?iv=" + base64(iv)`. La spec la marca como deprecada, pero NDK 2.12.2 la usa.

**NIP-01** (01.md:19-55): `id = sha256(utf8(json([0,pubkey,created_at,kind,tags,content])))` sin espacios. En `content` se escapan solo `\n \" \\ \r \t \b \f`. `sig` es Schnorr BIP-340 sobre los 32 bytes del id. Los kinds 20000-29999 son efímeros y el relay no los guarda (01.md:98).

**Relays** (prueba propia, script en `scratchpad/scripts/roundtrip.py`): REQ `#p` propio + EVENT 24133 firmado → eco recibido.
- `wss://relay.damus.io`: OK, 0,38 s. `wss://relay.primal.net`: OK, 0,35 s. `wss://nos.lol`: OK, 1,09 s.
- `wss://relay.nsec.app`: el DNS resuelve (65.109.67.137), pero **la conexión TCP/443 hace timeout** (también con curl). Puede ser la red local o una caída: no lo pude confirmar.

## 2. Flujo exacto SN ↔ bunker (contenido descifrado)

Sea `B` la pubkey del bunker (= usuario) y `C` la pubkey efímera de SN. Todos los eventos son `{"kind":24133,"pubkey":<emisor>,"tags":[["p",<receptor>]],"content":<cifrado>,...}`.

0. El bunker se suscribe: `["REQ","sub",{"kinds":[24133],"#p":["B"],"since":<ahora-10>}]`.
1. SN → bunker (**NIP-04**): `{"id":"k3j9x","method":"connect","params":["","<secret>"]}`
   Bunker → SN: `{"id":"k3j9x","result":"ack"}`
2. SN → bunker: `{"id":"a8f2q","method":"get_public_key","params":[]}` → `{"id":"a8f2q","result":"B"}`
3. SN → bunker:
   `{"id":"z1m0p","method":"sign_event","params":["{\"created_at\":1793750400,\"content\":\"Stacker News Authentication\",\"tags\":[[\"challenge\",\"<k1>\"],[\"u\",\"https://stacker.news\"],[\"method\",\"GET\"]],\"kind\":27235,\"pubkey\":\"B\",\"id\":\"<hex>\"}"]}`
   Si el usuario aprueba: `{"id":"z1m0p","result":"{\"id\":\"<hex>\",\"pubkey\":\"B\",\"created_at\":1793750400,\"kind\":27235,\"tags\":[...],\"content\":\"Stacker News Authentication\",\"sig\":\"<128 hex>\"}"}`
   Si rechaza: `{"id":"z1m0p","result":"","error":"usuario rechazó la firma"}`
4. `ping` (SN no lo usa en el login): `{"id":"..","method":"ping","params":[]}` → `{"id":"..","result":"pong"}`.
5. Método desconocido: `{"id":"..","result":"","error":"método no soportado: <m>"}`.

## 3. Supuestos sin verificar
- Que `NEXT_PUBLIC_URL` en producción sea `https://stacker.news`. El `.env.development` dice `http://localhost:3000`. No afecta: firmamos lo que llegue.
- Que el JS desplegado en stacker.news use la misma NDK 2.12.2 que el repo, y que SN no tenga un timeout en otra capa (por ejemplo en el k1). No encontré expiración del k1 en `pubkeyAuth`.
- El estado real de `relay.nsec.app`.
- Si damus, nos.lol o primal exigen NIP-42 a los eventos 24133 en el futuro. Hoy no lo exigen.

## 4. Recomendaciones mínimas
1. **Implementar el descifrado NIP-04 y el NIP-44 y responder con el mismo esquema del request** (`'?iv=' in content` → NIP-04). Sin NIP-04, el login con SN **no funciona**. NIP-04 son unas 10 líneas con `cryptography` (AES-CBC + PKCS7).
2. Responder `connect` siempre con `"ack"`. Ignorar `params[0]`, que puede venir vacío. Si el token lleva secret, validar `params[1]`, y al acertar registrar `C` como cliente autorizado y rotar el secret. Rechazar `sign_event` y `get_public_key` de un `C` no autorizado.
3. En `sign_event`: tomar del parámetro **solo** `kind, created_at, tags, content` sin modificarlos (ni reordenar tags). Poner `pubkey=B`, recalcular el id con `json.dumps([0,...], separators=(',',':'), ensure_ascii=False)` y firmar con `sign_schnorr`. Opcional: si el `id` que trae el request difiere del nuestro, devolver error, porque significa que el sig no le serviría a NDK.
4. Usar un solo relay: **`wss://relay.damus.io`** (verificado hoy). Dejarlo configurable y anotar `nos.lol` como alternativa. Mantener abierta la conexión WS, reconectar con backoff y re-enviar el REQ. Deduplicar por `event.id`.
5. Verificar id y firma de cada evento entrante antes de descifrarlo. Validar también `kind==24133`, que el `p` sea `B` y que no esté duplicado.
6. Tests: los vectores oficiales de NIP-44 (`get_conversation_key`, `encrypt_decrypt`, `calc_padded_len`) más un round-trip de NIP-04.

## 5. Riesgos y trampas
- **NIP-04 por defecto en NDK 2.12.2**, aunque la spec diga NIP-44. Es la trampa principal.
- **Devolver el secret en `connect`** (lo permite la spec) rompe el login con NDK: este exige `"ack"`.
- `coincurve.ecdh()` hashea. Usar `PublicKey(b'\x02'+B).multiply(sk).format()[1:33]`. Aplica a NIP-04 y a NIP-44.
- `cryptography`: el `ChaCha20` recibe un nonce de **16 bytes** = contador LE de 4 bytes + nonce de 12. Pasar `b'\x00'*4 + chacha_nonce`.
- Las pubkeys de Nostr son x-only (32 bytes). Para ECDH hay que anteponer `0x02`.
- Los eventos 24133 son efímeros: si el bunker no está suscrito cuando SN manda `connect`, el mensaje se pierde. Hay que arrancar el WS antes de mostrar el token. Si el `since` es demasiado estricto y hay desfase de reloj, se pierden eventos: usar un margen.
- Si el secret es de un solo uso y SN reintenta tras un fallo, `connect` falla. Hay que mostrar un token nuevo en la UI (SN ya sugiere "fresh token").
- La serialización del id debe ser idéntica a `JSON.stringify`. Con `ensure_ascii=False` y separadores compactos, Python coincide para todo texto normal; los surrogates sueltos son un caso borde despreciable.
- No loguear el `content` descifrado de `sign_event` junto con la clave, y nunca loguear el nsec.

```json
  "kdf": {"nombre": "scrypt", "n": 131072, "r": 8, "p": 1, "salt": "<b64 16 B>"},
  "cifrado": {"nombre": "chacha20poly1305", "nonce": "<b64 12 B>", "datos": "<b64 32 B + tag 16 B>"},
  "pubkey": "<hex x-only 32 B>"
}
```

- **scrypt n=2^17, r=8, p=1** (128 MiB, ~0,28 s en esta máquina) **[PROBADO]**. Tiempos medidos:
  2^15 0,07 s · 2^16 0,14 s · 2^17 0,28 s · 2^18 0,58 s. Se elige 2^17 (recomendación OWASP vigente es ≥ 2^17 con r=8);
  2^18 también cabe en el presupuesto de 1 s. Los parámetros se **leen del archivo**, así se pueden subir sin romper archivos viejos.
- **salt** 16 B y **nonce** 12 B con `os.urandom`, nuevos en cada guardado (nunca reutilizar nonce con la misma clave).
- **AAD** = `b"nostr-signer/clave/v1|" + pubkey_hex`. Así, si alguien edita `pubkey` o `version`, el descifrado falla
  (`InvalidTag`) **[PROBADO: AAD alterado → InvalidTag]**. Tras descifrar se verifica además que la pubkey derivada == `pubkey`.
- `pubkey` en claro permite mostrar "¿desbloquear la cuenta npub1…?" sin pedir contraseña (no es secreto).
- Escritura atómica: escribir `clave.json.tmp` y `os.replace()`. Contraseña mínima de 8 caracteres (validar en backend).

```python
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.scrypt import Scrypt
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import ChaCha20Poly1305
k = Scrypt(salt=salt, length=32, n=2**17, r=8, p=1).derive(contrasena.encode())  # objeto de un solo uso
datos = ChaCha20Poly1305(k).encrypt(nonce, secreto32, aad)   # devuelve ct||tag
secreto32 = ChaCha20Poly1305(k).decrypt(nonce, datos, aad)   # lanza cryptography.exceptions.InvalidTag
```

**Flujo**: al iniciar, si no existe `data/clave.json` la página ofrece "Generar" o "Pegar nsec" + contraseña (x2).
Si existe, pide solo la contraseña ("Desbloquear"). La clave queda en memoria del proceso mientras corre; nunca
vuelve al navegador. Contraseña incorrecta → mensaje genérico, con espera de ~1 s (scrypt ya la impone).
**Contraseña olvidada**: no hay recuperación (es la propiedad deseada). La UI ofrece "Olvidé la contraseña: borrar
la clave guardada y empezar de nuevo" (requiere confirmación; el usuario restaura con su nsec respaldado).
Correr scrypt con `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` para no bloquear el event loop (y el WebSocket del relay).

## 2. coincurve: ECDH sin hash y Schnorr

- `PrivateKey.ecdh(public_key)` **no tiene `hashfn`** en v21 (firma: `ecdh(self, public_key)`) y devuelve
  `sha256(punto comprimido)` **[PROBADO]**. Por eso **no sirve para NIP-44**.
- Coordenada X sin hashear **[PROBADO, vector oficial 1 de NIP-44 coincide]**:

```python
from coincurve import PrivateKey, PublicKey, PublicKeyXOnly
x_compartida = PublicKey(b"\x02" + pub_x_only).multiply(secreto32).format()[1:]   # 32 B
```
  (Anteponer `02` es correcto: el x de `k·P` no depende de la paridad de `P`. `multiply` usa
  `secp256k1_ec_pubkey_tweak_mul`, de tiempo constante.)
- Pubkey Nostr x-only: `PrivateKey(s).public_key.format()[1:]` == `PublicKeyXOnly.from_secret(s).format()` **[PROBADO]**.
- Firma BIP-340 **[PROBADO]**:
```python
sig = PrivateKey(s).sign_schnorr(id_evento_32B, os.urandom(32))   # 64 B; aux aleatorio recomendado
ok  = PublicKeyXOnly(pub_x).verify(sig, id_evento_32B)
```
  `sign_schnorr` firma el mensaje **tal cual** (no lo hashea): se le pasa el `id` (sha256 de la serialización NIP-01).
  El firmante **recalcula** el id; nunca confía en un `id` enviado por el cliente.

### NIP-44 v2 con `cryptography` **[PROBADO: conversation_key y payload del vector 1 idénticos; ida y vuelta OK]**

| Paso | Uso exacto |
|---|---|
| conversation_key = HKDF-Extract(salt="nip44-v2", IKM=x) | `hmac.HMAC(b"nip44-v2", hashes.SHA256())` + `update(x)` + `finalize()` (Extract = HMAC; la clase `HKDF` no expone solo Extract) |
| claves del mensaje | `HKDFExpand(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=76, info=nonce32).derive(conversation_key)` → `[0:32]` chacha_key, `[32:44]` chacha_nonce, `[44:76]` hmac_key |
| cifrar | `Cipher(algorithms.ChaCha20(chacha_key, b"\0\0\0\0" + chacha_nonce), mode=None).encryptor()` — nonce de 16 B = contador 4 B LE (0) + nonce 12 B |
| MAC | `hmac.HMAC(hmac_key, hashes.SHA256())`, `update(nonce32 + ciphertext)`; al descifrar usar `.verify(mac)` (tiempo constante) **antes** de descifrar |
| payload | `base64(0x02 ‖ nonce32 ‖ ct ‖ mac)`; padding `u16 BE largo ‖ texto ‖ ceros` según `calc_padded_len` |

Validaciones al descifrar: no empieza con `#`; largo base64 entre 132 y 87472; versión 2; MAC; largo de
padding exacto; texto 1..65535 bytes. Usar `ChaCha20Poly1305` **solo** para el archivo de clave, nunca en NIP-44.
(Si el experto de protocolo confirma que SN necesita NIP-04, ese sería AES-256-CBC con `algorithms.AES` + `modes.CBC`;
**[NO PROBADO]**, ojalá evitable.)

## 3. Modelo de amenazas (app local, un usuario)

| Amenaza | Medida mínima |
|---|---|
| Otro equipo de la red usa la API | `web.run_app(host="127.0.0.1")`, nunca `0.0.0.0` |
| Otra web abierta en el navegador llama a `127.0.0.1` (CSRF) | Toda acción es `POST` JSON con cabecera `X-Token` (token aleatorio `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` por arranque, inyectado en `index.html` al servirlo). Una cabecera propia fuerza preflight CORS que no respondemos → bloqueado. Además, si viene `Origin`, debe ser `http://127.0.0.1:PUERTO` o `http://localhost:PUERTO`. Comparar token con `hmac.compare_digest` |
| DNS rebinding (evil.com resuelve a 127.0.0.1) | Middleware que rechaza (403) si `Host` ∉ {`127.0.0.1:PUERTO`, `localhost:PUERTO`}. También en GET (el estado revela la npub y los pedidos) |
| Clickjacking / scripts externos | Cabeceras `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Cache-Control: no-store` en `/api/*`. Todo texto del evento se inserta con `textContent`, nunca `innerHTML` |
| Filtración de secretos | `nsec`, secreto hex, contraseña, conversation_key y **contenidos descifrados** nunca en logs. Se loguea solo `method`, `id` del pedido y pubkey del cliente abreviada. `repr()` de la clase de claves devuelve `<ClaveNostr npub1…>`. Log de aiohttp sin cuerpos |
| Cliente ajeno usa el bunker | `bunker://<pub>?relay=…&secret=<token_urlsafe(16)>`. `connect` exige `params[1] == secret` (compare_digest). El primer cliente válido queda como **único cliente autorizado**; el resto de métodos de otras pubkeys se ignoran/responden error. El secret se invalida tras usarse (botón "nuevo bunker" genera otro) |
| Firma no deseada | Cada `sign_event` va a la cola y requiere clic en "Aprobar". Se muestra `kind`, `content` (truncado), `tags` y `created_at`. Timeout de aprobación 120 s → respuesta `error: "rechazado"`. Máx. 5 pedidos pendientes |
| Mensajes enormes / malformados | Mensajes del relay > 128 KiB se descartan (`max_msg_size` en `ws_connect`). Payload NIP-44 con límites del estándar. JSON de RPC validado (tipos, `id` str, `params` lista). Eventos kind 24133 con `created_at` muy viejo (> 5 min) o `id` repetido se ignoran (anti-replay) y se verifica la firma del evento entrante |
| Caída del relay | Bucle de reconexión con backoff 1-2-4…30 s; al reconectar se re-suscribe con `since=ahora-10s`. Estado del relay visible en la UI |

**UI muestra**: npub, `bunker://` (con botón copiar), estado del relay, cliente conectado, pedidos pendientes e historial
breve. **No muestra**: contraseña, ni el nsec salvo **una vez al generarlo** (con "lo guardé" para continuar). No hay
"ver nsec" posterior (si se quiere, solo reingresando la contraseña; fuera de alcance).

**API local** (todo JSON, todo bajo `/api`, todo con `X-Token`):

| Ruta | Uso |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/estado` | `{fase: "sin_clave"|"bloqueado"|"listo", npub, bunker, relay: "conectado"|"reconectando", cliente, pendientes:[…]}` |
| `POST /api/crear` | `{contrasena, nsec?}` → si no hay nsec, genera; responde `{nsec}` **solo** si fue generado |

Sincronización: **polling** de `/api/estado` cada 1 s. Es lo más simple y robusto (sin reconexión de un segundo WS,
la página se recupera sola tras recargar). Pedido pendiente:
`{id: "<uuid corto local>", metodo: "sign_event", cliente: "npub1…", recibido: ts, expira: ts, evento: {kind, content, tags, created_at}}`.
En el backend es un `dict[id] -> (datos, asyncio.Future)`; `/api/responder` resuelve el Future y `firmante.py`
lo espera con `asyncio.wait_for(fut, 120)`.

# Mesa de diseño — 1. Protocolo Nostr (NIP-46 / NIP-44 / Stacker News)

Fuentes descargadas el 2026-11-04: `nips@master` (46.md, 44.md, 04.md, 01.md), `stackernews/stacker.news@27938a6` (2026-11-03), tarball `@nostr-dev-kit/ndk-2.12.2` (es la versión exacta del `package-lock.json` de SN, línea 6003).

## 1. Hechos verificados (con fuente)

**NIP-46**
- Token: `bunker://<remote-signer-pubkey-hex>?relay=<wss://...>&relay=...&secret=<opcional>` (46.md:45). El secret es de un solo uso: "SHOULD ignore new attempts ... with old secret" (46.md:48).
- Request y response son eventos `kind 24133`: el request lleva `tags [["p", remote-signer-pubkey]]` y el response lleva `[["p", client-pubkey]]` (46.md:69-78 y 137-148). El contenido es JSON `{id, method, params:[strings]}` / `{id, result, error?}` (46.md:82-88 y 152-158).
- `connect` recibe `[<remote-signer-pubkey>, <secret?>, <perms?>, <metadata?>]` y devuelve `"ack"` **o** el secret. `sign_event` recibe `[json(evento sin firmar)]` y devuelve `json_stringified(evento firmado)`. `ping` devuelve `"pong"` y `get_public_key` devuelve la pubkey hex (46.md:100-103).
- Los errores van en el campo `error` del response: su presencia indica el error. Un método desconocido "MUST be replied with an error" (46.md:162-164).
- La spec exige NIP-44 (46.md:80 y 150).
- La spec permite que la remote-signer-pubkey sea igual a la user-pubkey (46.md:23 y el ejemplo de 46.md:168-169).

**Stacker News (cliente)**
- `components/nostr-auth.js:122-163`: `createAuth()` → k1; `NDKNip46Signer(token)`; `blockUntilReady()`; luego firma este evento: `kind 27235`, `content "Stacker News Authentication"`, `tags [["challenge",k1],["u",NEXT_PUBLIC_URL],["method","GET"]]`, y `signIn('nostr', {event})`.
- `lib/nostr.js:197-201`: un parche cambia `bunker://` por `http://` antes de parsear la URL. `lib/nostr.js:42`: `clientName:'stacker.news'`, pero 27235 es efímero, así que NDK no agrega la tag `client` (ndk `src/events/index.ts:547-563`).
- Servidor `pages/api/auth/[...nextauth].js` (líneas 241-270 del archivo): recalcula `sha256(JSON.stringify([0,pubkey,created_at,kind,tags,content]))`, verifica Schnorr y **exige que `tags[0]` sea `["challenge", k1]`** (exactamente 2 elementos). Después borra el k1 (anti-replay, línea 207).
- No hay timeout: NDK espera sin límite y SN solo muestra una sugerencia a los 10 s (`nostr-auth.js:101-106` y 138).
- SN no agrega relays propios para NIP-46: usa solo los `relay=` del token (ndk `signers/nip46/rpc.ts:46-63`).

**NDK 2.12.2, lo que importa** (`src/signers/nip46/index.ts` y `rpc.ts`)
- **Cifrado por defecto: NIP-04.** `encryptionType = "nip04"` (rpc.ts:37). Todos los requests se cifran con ese valor (rpc.ts:206). Cambia a nip44 solo cuando llega un response sin `?iv=` (rpc.ts:109-112). Si falla el descifrado, prueba con el otro esquema (rpc.ts:119-129). **Conclusión: el primer `connect` llega cifrado con NIP-04.**
- Parámetros de connect: `[userPubkey ?? "", secret?]` (index.ts:172-174). `userPubkey` sale del parámetro `pubkey=` del token (index.ts:101). Como nuestro token no lo lleva, **`params[0]` llega como `""`**, no como nuestra pubkey.
- **Exige `result === "ack"`.** Si se devuelve el secret, el login se rechaza (index.ts:184-191).
- Después del ack llama a `get_public_key` y usa `response.result` sin revisar `error` (index.ts:198-213).
- `sign()` manda `[JSON.stringify(rawEvent)]`, que incluye `pubkey` e `id` ya calculados por NDK, y **solo usa `json.sig` del response** (index.ts:256-273 y events/index.ts:429-441). NDK conserva su propio id, created_at y pubkey.
- Suscripción del cliente: `{kinds:[24133], "#p":[client-pubkey]}`, sin `since` (index.ts:132-135). El id del request es `Math.random().toString(36).substring(7)` (rpc.ts:182).
- Los relays del token reciben una `authPolicy` NIP-42 signIn (rpc.ts:60).

**NIP-44 v2** (44.md:68-99 y 233-282)
1. `shared_x` = coordenada X de `a·B`, **sin hashear** (44.md:71-72 y 160). `conversation_key = HKDF-extract(sha256, IKM=shared_x, salt=b"nip44-v2")`.
2. `nonce` = 32 bytes aleatorios. `HKDF-expand(PRK=conversation_key, info=nonce, L=76)` → `chacha_key[0:32]`, `chacha_nonce[32:44]` y `hmac_key[44:76]`.
3. Padding: prefijo u16 BE con el largo, luego el texto y luego ceros hasta `calc_padded_len` (mínimo 32; potencias de 2, en chunks de 32 o de next_pow/8). Desde 65536 bytes el prefijo es de 6 bytes, pero no nos aplica.
4. ChaCha20 (RFC 8439) con contador 0. `mac = HMAC-SHA256(hmac_key, nonce || ciphertext)`.
5. `base64(0x02 || nonce || ciphertext || mac)` con padding. Al descifrar: si empieza con `#` → versión no soportada; se exigen al menos 132 caracteres y 99 bytes; la MAC se compara en tiempo constante.
- Vectores: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paulmillr/nip44/main/nip44.vectors.json`. El sha256 que da la spec (44.md:303) es `269ed0f69e4c192512cc779e78c555090cebc7c785b609e338a62afc3ce25040`, y **coincide con el archivo descargado hoy**.

**NIP-04** (04.md:13 y 19-45): AES-256-CBC (PKCS7). La clave es `shared_x` sin hashear y el IV es de 16 bytes aleatorios. Formato: `base64(ct) + "?iv=" + base64(iv)`. La spec la marca como deprecada, pero NDK 2.12.2 la usa.

**NIP-01** (01.md:19-55): `id = sha256(utf8(json([0,pubkey,created_at,kind,tags,content])))` sin espacios. En `content` se escapan solo `\n \" \\ \r \t \b \f`. `sig` es Schnorr BIP-340 sobre los 32 bytes del id. Los kinds 20000-29999 son efímeros y el relay no los guarda (01.md:98).

**Relays** (prueba propia, script en `scratchpad/scripts/roundtrip.py`): REQ `#p` propio + EVENT 24133 firmado → eco recibido.
- `wss://relay.damus.io`: OK, 0,38 s. `wss://relay.primal.net`: OK, 0,35 s. `wss://nos.lol`: OK, 1,09 s.
- `wss://relay.nsec.app`: el DNS resuelve (65.109.67.137), pero **la conexión TCP/443 hace timeout** (también con curl). Puede ser la red local o una caída: no lo pude confirmar.

## 2. Flujo exacto SN ↔ bunker (contenido descifrado)

Sea `B` la pubkey del bunker (= usuario) y `C` la pubkey efímera de SN. Todos los eventos son `{"kind":24133,"pubkey":<emisor>,"tags":[["p",<receptor>]],"content":<cifrado>,...}`.

0. El bunker se suscribe: `["REQ","sub",{"kinds":[24133],"#p":["B"],"since":<ahora-10>}]`.
1. SN → bunker (**NIP-04**): `{"id":"k3j9x","method":"connect","params":["","<secret>"]}`
   Bunker → SN: `{"id":"k3j9x","result":"ack"}`
2. SN → bunker: `{"id":"a8f2q","method":"get_public_key","params":[]}` → `{"id":"a8f2q","result":"B"}`
3. SN → bunker:
   `{"id":"z1m0p","method":"sign_event","params":["{\"created_at\":1793750400,\"content\":\"Stacker News Authentication\",\"tags\":[[\"challenge\",\"<k1>\"],[\"u\",\"https://stacker.news\"],[\"method\",\"GET\"]],\"kind\":27235,\"pubkey\":\"B\",\"id\":\"<hex>\"}"]}`
   Si el usuario aprueba: `{"id":"z1m0p","result":"{\"id\":\"<hex>\",\"pubkey\":\"B\",\"created_at\":1793750400,\"kind\":27235,\"tags\":[...],\"content\":\"Stacker News Authentication\",\"sig\":\"<128 hex>\"}"}`
   Si rechaza: `{"id":"z1m0p","result":"","error":"usuario rechazó la firma"}`
4. `ping` (SN no lo usa en el login): `{"id":"..","method":"ping","params":[]}` → `{"id":"..","result":"pong"}`.
5. Método desconocido: `{"id":"..","result":"","error":"método no soportado: <m>"}`.
